property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner, after calling setOwner(x) the contract's owner equals the provided x; the mutant instead ignores the provided x and sets owner to msg.sender, violating this rule for inputs where x != msg.sender.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) sets owner() to the provided newOwner (i.e. owner() == newOwner after the call); the mutant instead sets owner() to msg.sender, so when newOwner != msg.sender the mutant violates this rule.
For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) updates C.owner() to exactly x; the mutant always clears owner to address(0) and thus violates this rule for inputs where x != address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates the contract's owner to exactly _owner; the mutant that deletes the assignment violates this because owner remains unchanged for some inputs.

The reference contract enforces that only the current owner can call setOwner (calls from the owner succeed and update owner), whereas the mutant allows only non-owners and thus will not let the owner call setOwner — so for any caller equal to the current owner, calling setOwner should succeed and update owner in the reference but the mutant will reject such calls.

For any address caller equal to the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) succeeds and updates owner to newOwner in the reference; the mutant inverts the guard and will revert such calls, so the property is that owner can call setOwner to change owner (caller==owner implies call succeeds and owner becomes the supplied address).

For all callers and input addresses, only the current owner may cause owner to change via setOwner (i.e., after any call to setOwner(x) when invoked by addr, c.owner() == addr implies the call succeeded and changed owner only if addr was the prior owner); the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to change owner, so there exist callers/newOwner inputs that make c.owner() differ between reference and mutant.

For any caller address a and target newOwner, only the current owner can change owner via setOwner (i.e., after a call by a, c.owner() == a iff a was the prior owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so a non-owner can become owner — the test fuzzes caller and newOwner and detects when a non-owner successfully changes owner.

The owner can only be changed by the immediate caller (msg.sender) — i.e., calling setOwner from an EOA or via a contract call only succeeds when that caller is the current owner; the mutant using tx.origin allows a different contract caller (where msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to bypass the guard, so the mutant can change owner in scenarios where the original cannot.

For any caller address X and target newOwner Y, only a direct call from the current owner (msg.sender == owner) can successfully change owner; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows a non-owner contract caller (msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to change owner, violating this rule.

For all callers, only a call whose immediate caller (msg.sender) equals the current owner can change owner via setOwner; the mutant that uses tx.origin can allow a non-owner contract (msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to change owner, violating this rule.

For all callers, only when msg.sender equals the current owner does setOwner succeed (i.e., setOwner can only be executed by the immediate caller being owner); the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows a non-owner contract to call setOwner successfully if tx.origin is the owner, violating this rule.

For all callers, setOwner only succeeds when the immediate caller (msg.sender) is the current owner; the mutant that uses tx.origin can let a non-owner contract (msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) succeed and change owner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address argument, calling setOwner succeeds and returns true in the correct contract; the mutant returns false for at least some such calls, breaking the rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(_owner) always returns true (reference guarantees a true success flag); the mutant returns (owner==_owner) which can be false when the new owner equals a different address transition, so the mutant can return false for some inputs while the reference always returns true.

For any caller msg.sender that is the current owner, calling setOwner(_owner) always returns true in the reference contract; the mutant returns (owner==_owner) which can be false for some fuzzed _owner values, so the mutant can cause setOwner to return false while the reference always returns true.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) completes and the reference C always returns true; the mutant returns (owner==_owner) which can be false for some _owner, so the mutant will produce a false return for some fuzzed _owner while the reference always returns true.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) MUST return true (reference always returns true); the mutant may return false when owner==_owner check yields false after assignment, so it violates this rule for some fuzzed _owner values.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) always returns true in the reference implementation; the mutant can return false for some fuzzed _owner (when the mutated return uses owner==_owner after assignment), so the rule is violated for some inputs.

For all callers, only the current owner can change the owner via setOwner — the reference enforces this (non-owner calls do not change owner), while the mutant allows any caller to overwrite owner and thus violates this invariant for some caller addresses.

For any caller address, the correct contract C allows the current owner (the address stored in owner) to successfully call setOwner and update owner; the mutant restricts onlyOwner to accept address(0) so some callers (including the current owner) will be unable to call setOwner and the call will revert or not change owner.
